segments.text: This is a saltwater crocodile, in Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve. Nothing here hunts it. It is an apex predator. But all its energy came from somewhere. Let's rewind!

First, last time's question. Why does your face turn red after running? Your working muscles make a lot of heat. So your body sends more blood close to your skin, to let the heat out. That's why your face turns red.

Welcome to TheOneApp, Explored! Today, you'll learn three things. First, what a food chain is. Second, about producers, consumers, predators and prey. And third, where every food chain begins. Let's get started!

Here's a Singapore fact. Saltwater crocodiles are the largest reptiles in the world, and a few live wild in Singapore's mangroves. At Sungei Buloh, visitors stay on the paths and keep a safe distance.
Did you feel that rewind? The crocodile ate a mudskipper. The mudskipper ate a crab. The crab ate a fallen mangrove leaf. And the leaf made its food from sunlight.

Now for the textbook link! In Primary Six, you learn about food chains. A food chain shows who eats whom. Green plants are producers: they make their own food using light energy. Animals are consumers: they eat plants or other animals. An animal that hunts is a predator, and the animal it hunts is its prey. The arrows in a food chain show the way energy flows: from the food, to the eater.
So here's the big idea. Almost every food chain begins with the Sun. Even a crocodile runs on sunlight!
Try this at home! Make a food chain from your school garden, or from your dinner. Start with the Sun, and draw the arrows the way energy flows.
Think about it! What would happen to the crocodile if all the mangrove crabs disappeared? I'll tell you the answer next time.
So remember. A food chain shows who eats whom. The arrows show the way energy flows. And almost every food chain begins with the Sun. Next time: the mosquitoes that fight dengue!
